title: Truly subquadratic \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation of edit distance
formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), do there exist real constants \(\delta_\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(K_\varepsilon>0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_\varepsilon\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\) and every pair of length-\(n\) strings \(x,y\), every execution uses at most \(K_\varepsilon(n+2)^{2-\delta_\varepsilon}\) word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance, the alphabet and computational model are specified below, and probability is over independent internal random bits for each fixed input pair.
definitions:
The input consists of \(n\geq1\) and two explicit arrays \(x,y\in\Sigma_n^n\), where \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). Each symbol occupies one word. The arrays and length are stored in consecutive input cells. Binary and any fixed alphabet are included, after relabeling the symbols. No compressed representation, access oracle, prior preprocessing or input distribution is supplied.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of edits in a sequence transforming \(x\) into \(y\), where one edit inserts one symbol of \(\Sigma_n\), deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol for another. Each costs one, and an equal-symbol match costs zero. Intermediate strings may have different lengths. There are no block edits, transpositions, symbol weights or affine gap penalties. In particular, a substitution costs one rather than an insertion plus a deletion. The minimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

For each fixed accuracy, the algorithm may choose a fixed integer \(B_\varepsilon\geq3\) and uses words of
\[w=B_\varepsilon\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
bits. Words represent unsigned integers modulo \(2^w\); memory is addressed by words, and all non-input cells start at zero. The program is a finite list of instructions and integer constants independent of \(n,x,y\). One instruction can read or write one word, compare words, branch, perform a bitwise Boolean operation, shift a word, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or compute an integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. Shifts discard overflow and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Address arithmetic has the same cost. Larger integers require several words and several charged instructions. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one instruction. All preprocessing, random draws and output writing are charged; no arbitrary-precision, oracle, advice or quantum instruction is available. The bound in the statement holds on every random-bit sequence, including executions with an incorrect answer, and forces termination.

The output is an integer written in signed binary notation. A successful execution must satisfy the displayed interval; a failed execution may output an integer outside it. Only the estimate is required, not a sequence of edits. Success must hold separately on every input pair, including identical strings and pairs at distance one. No additive error term is allowed.

The accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before choosing the algorithm, the word-size constant, the exponent saving and the runtime constant. They may all depend on \(\varepsilon\), but never on \(n\) or the strings. Thus the order is \(\forall\varepsilon\;\exists A_\varepsilon,B_\varepsilon,\delta_\varepsilon,K_\varepsilon\;\forall n,x,y\). No one positive exponent saving must work for all accuracies. The accuracy is not a varying input to a common algorithm, and no effective procedure generating these algorithms, or bound polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), is required. The term truly subquadratic means the positive saving \(\delta_\varepsilon\) remains fixed as \(n\) grows; savings such as a fixed power of \(\log n\) do not suffice.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full existence statement for every fixed rational accuracy, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must prove that for some fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), no permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant achieve the per-input multiplicative guarantee with any positive fixed exponent saving and any fixed runtime constant. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the stated randomized algorithms. A conditional lower bound settles only the corresponding conditional claim unless its hypothesis is also proved. One fixed coarse approximation factor, a bound with only a subpolynomial saving from quadratic time, an expected-time guarantee alone, or a theorem for restricted input pairs is insufficient. This is an algorithm-existence target with the stated relative accuracy, not a numerical target with a separate additive tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Rubinstein explicitly posed this in Open question 2 of his July 2018 exposition, with near-linear time as a further possibility. His May 2020 update resolves the separate constant-factor question, not the arbitrary-accuracy question. The present card keeps the truly subquadratic branch, with accuracy chosen before the positive exponent saving.

For example, fixing \(\varepsilon=1/100\) asks for a one-percent relative estimate and some positive exponent saving that remains fixed at all lengths. The saving may become smaller at other, more demanding accuracies. Therefore the claim does not require a fixed subquadratic algorithm for exact distance. Choosing an accuracy below \(1/n\) to force exactness instead makes the accuracy depend on the input length, which the theorem does not allow.

Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 theorem gives \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) in stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). Theorem 6.1 and footnote 21 give success at least \(1-1/n\) when \(n\) denotes total string length. This is a substantial improvement beyond fixed logarithmic savings, but its stated guarantee does not establish a fixed positive saving in the quadratic exponent. The result is for unit-cost edit distance; its separate LCS guarantee concerns another objective.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a constant approximation factor in \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) time for each fixed \(\eta>0\). Their Theorem 1.1 permits the approximation factor to depend on \(\eta\); the following paragraph describes it as doubly exponential in \(1/\eta\). It is not a guarantee of \(1+\varepsilon\) for a prescribed small \(\varepsilon\). The paper’s August 2026 journal publication retains this different accuracy–time tradeoff.

Backurs and Indyk show that a fixed exponent saving for exact edit distance would yield a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. Their reduction provides conditional evidence against fast exact computation. It does not itself yield a fixed multiplicative-accuracy lower bound or an unconditional impossibility theorem for this card.

The retained TCS-6624 asks for any fixed constant factor in \(O(n(\log(n+2))^d)\) time with fixed \(d\). A positive answer here would not supply that runtime, while such a coarse fast estimate would not supply arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. TCS-7235 asks for the stronger near-exact bound \(n^{1+o(1)}\). Its positive answer would imply the target here, but a fixed saving from exponent two does not imply an exponent approaching one. These approved targets remain separate.

Purely multiplicative accuracy constrains small distances as well. If \(\operatorname{ED}=0\), the successful output is zero. If \(\operatorname{ED}=1\) and \(\varepsilon<1\), its integer output must be one. Thus a growing additive error or a guarantee only for distant pairs does not meet the question. Weighted edits, tree structures, codeword promises and random-input models likewise have different hypotheses.

why: This asks whether any fixed tolerance for a relative alignment error permits a fixed polynomial saving from the quadratic time scale on arbitrary sequences. Exact edit distance has strong conditional hardness evidence, while fast coarse approximations already exist. The question isolates whether near-exact approximation can cross the fixed-exponent boundary for every desired fixed accuracy.

importance.reason: A longstanding central accuracy–runtime question for edit distance, explicitly posed before the constant-factor breakthroughs and sharpened by the 2026 approximation scheme. Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.

progress.text: Backurs–Indyk establish the conditional strongly subquadratic barrier for exact edit distance.
Rubinstein poses the arbitrary-accuracy truly subquadratic question separately from constant-factor approximation.
Andoni–Nosatzki announce constant-factor approximation with every fixed positive runtime slack; the later full revision is dated 14 July 2022.
Mao–Rubinstein announce a randomized near-exact approximation scheme with a quasipolynomial improvement over quadratic time, subsequently published at STOC 2026.
The Andoni–Nosatzki journal article is published online with its fixed-slack constant-factor guarantee.

sentences: Unit-cost edit distance counts insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform one string into another.
The question asks whether every fixed positive relative tolerance permits a randomized approximation with a positive fixed saving from the quadratic time exponent.
Both the algorithm and the exponent saving may depend on the tolerance but must work on every explicitly stored pair with the stated per-input success probability.
The 2026 approximation scheme gives a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time without establishing this fixed-exponent guarantee.
The target remains distinct from fast coarse approximation and is implied by the stronger retained almost-linear near-exact question.
